❯ project 01
GNSS Receiver & Resilience
Pull position and time out of signals from 20,000 km up — and learn how they're attacked

$50
beginner
1 weekend
↗ open in Blueprint
As-built desktop unit — ESP32 + u-blox NEO-6M + RTL-SDR Blog V4, GPS patch antenna on the lid.
cost — ~$50 as built · the NEO-6M core alone is ~$20
## why this matters
Every ship, aircraft, drone, and vehicle depends on GNSS for position and precise time, which makes it one of the most important — and most
contested — signals in defense. Building a receiver is the way in: a $12 module locks onto satellites 20,000 km overhead and hands you latitude,
longitude, altitude, and nanosecond-grade time, and with an SDR you can even glimpse the raw signal buried below the noise floor. Understanding
how GNSS works, and why it is so fragile, is foundational to positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) engineering — one of the largest and most
strategically vital areas of defense EE.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand GNSS fundamentals (trilateration from time-of-flight, the role of precise time), NMEA data, why the signal sits below the noise floor
and how correlation recovers it, and the concepts of jamming and spoofing resilience. PNT is core defense and aerospace EE.

→ the job this maps to: positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) engineering — aerospace, defense, autonomous-
systems, and timing-infrastructure teams.
! RECEIVE ONLY — NEVER JAM OR SPOOF
This build only listens. Jamming or spoofing GNSS is a serious federal crime and endangers aircraft, ships, and emergency services, so nothing
here transmits and the resilience discussion stays conceptual. Understanding the threat is a defensive skill; creating it is not.

defense signals — a Build List field guide
02 / 23
## how it works

▸
Trilateration from time: Each satellite broadcasts its position and an extremely precise time. The receiver measures how long each signal took to

arrive, converts that to a distance, and solves for its own position where the ranges intersect — needing at least four satellites to also solve for its
own clock error.

▸
Time is the real product: Because position comes from timing, GNSS is first a time system. The satellites carry atomic clocks and the receiver
recovers time to nanoseconds — which is why GNSS quietly synchronises power grids, cell networks, and financial systems, and why time itself is a
defense priority.

▸
Below the noise floor: The signal arriving at your antenna is weaker than the background noise. The receiver recovers it by correlating against each
satellite's known pseudo-random code (a spread-spectrum trick) — a huge processing gain that pulls the signal up out of the noise.

▸
Reading the output: A receiver module outputs standard NMEA sentences over serial: position, altitude, speed, satellites in view, and fix quality.
Parsing these is your window into what the receiver is actually doing.

▸
Why it is fragile: The received power is tiny, so a small interferer can jam it, and because the format is public, a fake stronger signal can spoof it. Real
systems defend with directional and adaptive antennas, multi-constellation receivers, and spoofing detection — the resilience side of PNT.

2
Parse NMEA
Read the NMEA sentences and extract latitude, longitude, altitude, speed, satellites in view, and fix quality. Print them cleanly and confirm they

3
Log a track
Record position over time and plot it (a walk around the block). See the accuracy, the noise, and how it degrades indoors or under cover.

4
Recover precise time
Use the receiver's timing output (the PPS pin, if present) and note how tightly it disciplines time — the feature that makes GNSS a synchronisation

With an RTL-SDR and an active antenna, tune to L1 (1575.42 MHz) and observe what looks like pure noise — then read how correlation pulls the real
signal out. That gap between 'looks like noise' and 'carries the world's timing' is the whole lesson.

❯ project 02
RF Direction Finder
Point a needle straight at a hidden transmitter — the core of signals intelligence

$185
advanced
1–2 weekends
↗ open in Blueprint
As-built rotational DF station — 144 MHz Yagi on a tripod, RTL-SDR Blog V4 feeding a Raspberry Pi 4.
cost — ~$185 as built (Pi 4 + 144 MHz Yagi + tripod) · from ~$45 with an RTL-SDR, Yagi and your own laptop
## why this matters
Finding where a radio signal comes from is one of the oldest and most important jobs in defense electronics — search and rescue, spectrum
enforcement, electronic warfare, and signals intelligence all rest on it. Build a direction finder and you can watch a bearing swing to point straight at a
hidden transmitter across a field. The accessible version uses a single SDR with a directional antenna and signal strength, or a pseudo-Doppler
array; the serious version uses a coherent multi-channel SDR to compute true angle-of-arrival from phase. It is the marquee build of this guide —
visual, deeply technical, and a direct window into how SIGINT and EW systems locate emitters.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand direction-finding techniques (RSSI / rotational, pseudo-Doppler, and phase-based angle-of-arrival), coherent multi-channel
reception, antenna arrays, and the math that turns antenna phase differences into a bearing. Coherent RF and DF are advanced, in-demand skills
across SIGINT, EW, and spectrum work.
→ the job this maps to: signals intelligence, electronic warfare, and spectrum engineering — defense RF, spectrum-
monitoring, and search-and-rescue teams.
! LOCATE, DON'T INTRUDE
This is receive-only: you locate transmitters, you never transmit or interfere. Use it for fox-hunting, tracking down interference, or search-and-
rescue beacons, and respect privacy and radio law — don't use it to covertly track people.

defense signals — a Build List field guide
05 / 23
## how it works

▸
The basic idea: A directional antenna hears a signal loudest when pointed at its source. Rotate it (or steer a phased array electronically) and the
direction of peak strength, or of a specific phase relationship, points back toward the transmitter.

▸
RSSI and rotational DF: The simplest method reads received signal strength as you rotate a Yagi; the peak is the bearing. Cheap and intuitive, but
reflections and multipath in real environments blur it, which is why better methods exist.

▸
Pseudo-Doppler: Rapidly switching between antennas arranged in a circle imposes a Doppler-like modulation whose phase encodes the arrival
angle. It works with a single receiver and is a classic, affordable DF technique.

▸
Phase-based angle-of-arrival: With multiple coherent receivers sharing one clock, you measure the tiny phase difference of the same signal
arriving at spaced antennas. That phase difference maps directly to the arrival angle — the method behind precise, modern DF.

▸
From one bearing to a fix: A single bearing is a line; take bearings from two or more locations and where they cross is the transmitter's position.
Moving receivers, or multiple stations, turn a direction into a location.
BUILD NOTE
Start cheap: one RTL-SDR and a directional (Yagi) antenna plus signal strength, or a pseudo-Doppler array. A coherent KrakenSDR is the upgrade
that gives true phase-based angle-of-arrival — far more robust, and worth it once the basics click.
## key design decisions

→
Why coherent multi-channel over a spinning antenna? A rotating Yagi with RSSI is cheap but slow and easily fooled by reflections, which create

false peaks in real environments. Coherent receivers measure phase across a fixed array instantly and are far more robust to multipath — which is
why professional DF uses phase-based angle-of-arrival, not a spinning antenna.

→
Why does coherence (a shared clock) matter so much? Phase-based DF depends on comparing the exact phase of the same signal at several
antennas. If the receivers don't share a clock, their phases drift independently and the comparison is meaningless. Locking them to one reference is
the entire reason a coherent SDR works where independent dongles do not.

→
Why does one direction finder only give a line, not a point? A single station measures the angle a signal arrives from, which defines a bearing line

— the transmitter is somewhere along it. Only by crossing bearings from different locations (or moving) does the intersection reveal the actual
position, which is why DF networks and moving platforms exist.

## wiring at a glance
SIGNAL & POWER CONNECTIONS
→ VHF Yagi (144 MHz) → RTL-SDR RF input via coax (SMA), shield to GND
→ RTL-SDR Blog V4 → Raspberry Pi 4 over USB (data + 5 V)

## build steps

1
Pick a method and a target
Choose RSSI-with-Yagi (cheapest), pseudo-Doppler, or coherent DF. Pick a legal, known test transmitter — a friend with a handheld, or a licensed
beacon — to hunt.

2
Build the antenna or array
Build or buy a Yagi for your band, or assemble the circular antenna array for coherent DF. Antenna geometry directly determines your accuracy.

3
Get a bearing
For RSSI, rotate and log signal strength versus heading; the peak is the bearing. For coherent, run the DF software and read the computed angle-of-
arrival. Confirm it points sensibly at the known source.

4
Handle multipath
Move around and watch reflections create false bearings, then average, change location, or switch to a phase-based method to firm up the estimate.
This is where DF gets real.

5
Triangulate to a fix
Take bearings from two or three separate spots, draw the lines on a map, and find the intersection. You've located the transmitter — the essence of
DF.

❯ project 03
Magnetic Anomaly Detector
Sense a hidden vehicle by the dent it makes in Earth's magnetic field

$52
intermediate
1 weekend
↗ open in Blueprint
As-built gradiometer — two matched HMC5883L magnetometers on the ends of a non-magnetic boom, ESP32 + OLED at centre.
cost — ~$52 as built · a two-sensor gradiometer on a non-magnetic boom
## why this matters
A large steel object — a vehicle, a pipe, a ship — distorts the Earth's magnetic field around it, and a sensitive magnetometer can detect that
distortion from a distance, with no contact and no emission. This is magnetic anomaly detection (MAD), used in defense for submarine hunting and
mine detection, and in the civilian world for archaeology, geophysics, and utility locating. Building one teaches you to pull a tiny anomaly out of a
large, noisy background field — a purely passive sensing skill with the same signal-in-noise flavour as the RF work, but in the magnetic domain.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand magnetometry (fluxgate and magnetoresistive sensors), the Earth's field as a baseline, gradiometry to cancel common-mode drift,
calibration, and anomaly detection against a noisy background. Passive magnetic sensing is used across defense, geophysics, and navigation.
→ the job this maps to: magnetic sensing and geophysical engineering — defense sensor, survey, navigation, and
instrumentation teams.
## how it works

▸
The Earth's field as baseline: The geomagnetic field is roughly 25–65 microtesla everywhere. A ferrous object perturbs it locally by a tiny amount,
so detecting the object means measuring that small change against the large steady baseline.

▸
Measuring the field: A fluxgate or magnetoresistive magnetometer outputs the field along each axis. Cheap 3-axis modules resolve well under a
microtesla — enough to see a car-sized anomaly at short range.

defense signals — a Build List field guide
09 / 23

▸
Anomaly, not absolute: What matters is the deviation from the local baseline. You establish the ambient field, then watch for the perturbation as a
ferrous mass comes near — the anomaly is the signal.

▸
Gradiometry kills drift: The baseline itself wanders with temperature, solar activity, and nearby currents. Two matched sensors a fixed distance
apart, subtracted, reject that shared drift and respond only to the steep local gradient of a nearby object.

▸
Range and mass: The anomaly falls off steeply with distance (roughly as the cube), so detection range depends on the object's mass and your
sensitivity. Understanding that falloff sets realistic expectations for any magnetic sensor.
BUILD NOTE

A single magnetometer drifts with temperature and Earth-field changes. Use two identical sensors as a gradiometer — subtracting one from the
other cancels the common background and leaves the local anomaly, the trick that makes real MAD work.

## build steps

1
Read the field
Wire a 3-axis magnetometer over I2C and read the field magnitude. Move a steel tool near it and watch the reading jump — your first anomaly.

2
Establish a baseline
Log the ambient field in a clear area and note how much it drifts over minutes. This baseline noise sets the smallest anomaly you can trust.

3
Build a gradiometer
Mount two matched sensors on a non-magnetic boom a fixed distance apart and subtract their readings. Confirm the common drift cancels while a
nearby object still shows up strongly.

4
Sweep for objects
Walk the gradiometer over the ground (or past a parked car) and log the gradient. Watch a clear peak appear over buried or nearby ferrous mass.

5
Map an anomaly
Take readings on a grid and plot the field or gradient as a heatmap, revealing the shape and location of the hidden mass. That map is the deliverable.

❯ project 04
Seismic Unattended Ground Sensor
Feel footsteps and vehicles through the ground before you can see them

$42
intermediate
1 weekend
↗ open in Blueprint
As-built ground sensor — SM-24 geophone and AD623 amp sealed in an IP65 body, driven into the ground on an M8 spike.
cost — ~$42 as built · SM-24 geophone + AD623 + ESP32 in a sealed IP65 box
## why this matters
Long before you can see or hear an approaching person or vehicle, the ground carries their vibration. A geophone — the same sensor used in oil
exploration and earthquake monitoring — turns that ground motion into a voltage, and with the right processing you can detect footsteps, tell a
person from a vehicle, and estimate direction. This is the principle behind unattended ground sensors used for perimeter monitoring. It is a passive,
emission-free build that teaches low-frequency signal detection, simple classification, and the reality of picking a faint signal out of environmental
noise.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand seismic and vibration sensing, very-low-frequency signal conditioning, event detection and simple classification (footstep versus
vehicle by frequency and cadence), and sensor siting. Passive ground sensing is used in perimeter security, seismology, and structural monitoring.

→ the job this maps to: unattended-sensor and perimeter-security engineering — defense sensor, seismic-monitoring,
and structural-health teams.
! YOUR OWN PERIMETER
This is passive monitoring of ground you own or are responsible for — a driveway, a fence line, a site perimeter. Keep it on your own property and
respect the privacy of anyone nearby; it senses motion, not identity.
## how it works

▸
The geophone: A geophone is a coil-and-magnet transducer that outputs a voltage proportional to ground velocity. Footsteps and vehicles couple
energy into the ground as low-frequency waves the geophone picks up.

defense signals — a Build List field guide
12 / 23

▸
The frequency band: Seismic events of interest live at low frequencies — footsteps a few to tens of Hz, vehicles lower and more continuous.
Amplify and band-pass this range while rejecting wind, mains hum, and higher-frequency noise.

▸
Detecting an event: A footstep is a short impulsive burst; the detector watches signal energy rise above the background floor and flags an event,
much like triggering on a noise-adaptive threshold.

▸
Classifying the source: A person produces distinct, spaced impulses at a walking cadence; a vehicle produces continuous, lower-frequency
energy. Looking at frequency content and rhythm lets you tell them apart — simple classification from a single sensor.

▸
Siting and range: Coupling to firm ground, sensor depth, and soil type dominate range and sensitivity. Where and how you plant the sensor matters
as much as the electronics — the practical heart of unattended sensing.

❯ project 05
Drone Detection Receiver
Spot a drone by the radio it can't stop transmitting — passive counter-UAS

$500
advanced
1–2 weekends
↗ open in Blueprint
As-built counter-UAS receiver — HackRF One + Raspberry Pi 4, motorised pan/tilt directional antenna, status LCD. Receive-only.
cost — ~$500 as built (HackRF One + Pi 4 + pan/tilt) · from ~$40 with an RTL-SDR for 2.4 GHz only
## why this matters
Small drones have gone from novelty to a serious security concern, and detecting them is now a major defense and infrastructure problem. Most
drones constantly transmit — a control link on 2.4 or 5.8 GHz and usually a video downlink — and those emissions are a fingerprint you can detect
passively with an SDR. Building a drone-detection receiver teaches you to scan the ISM bands, recognise the signatures of drone control and video
protocols, and flag a drone's presence without transmitting anything yourself. It is a receive-only, topical build that sits right at the centre of the fast-
growing counter-UAS field.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand wideband spectrum scanning, recognising signal signatures (frequency-hopping control links, video downlinks), the ISM bands
drones use, and energy and feature detection — the passive-sensing core of counter-UAS. It maps directly onto RF-sensing and spectrum-
awareness roles.
→ the job this maps to: counter-UAS and RF-sensing engineering — drone-defense, critical-infrastructure-protection,
and spectrum-monitoring teams.
! DETECT ONLY — NEVER JAM OR HIJACK
This build never transmits. Jamming, hijacking, or spoofing a drone or its GPS is illegal in most countries and can be dangerous, so this stays
entirely passive — you sense that a drone is present, nothing more. Respect privacy and spectrum law.

defense signals — a Build List field guide
15 / 23
## how it works

▸
Drones are noisy on purpose: A drone needs a control link and usually a live video feed, so it is almost always transmitting on 2.4 GHz, 5.8 GHz, or
both. Those emissions are exactly what a passive receiver looks for.

▸
Scanning the bands: An SDR sweeps the ISM bands and builds a spectrogram, or waterfall. Drone control links often frequency-hop across the
band in a recognisable pattern, and video downlinks appear as wide, steady carriers.

▸
Signatures, not just energy: Distinguishing a drone from WiFi and Bluetooth means recognising the shape and timing of its signals — the hopping
cadence of the control link, the bandwidth of the video — rather than just seeing energy in the band.

▸
Detection and alerting: When a matching signature appears, you flag it. Advanced systems classify the drone type from its protocol fingerprint; a
first build can simply and reliably say 'a drone-like signal is present.'

▸
Range and antennas: A directional antenna extends range and, swept, hints at direction. Combined with the direction finder from project 2, passive
detection can become passive location — all without emitting a thing.

## why this matters
In contested environments, communications have to survive both interception and interference, and the classic answers are spread spectrum and
encryption. Build a data link that hops across many frequencies in a pattern only the two endpoints know, and encrypts every packet with AES, and
you have a channel that is hard to jam, hard to intercept, and hard to even detect — the same principles behind military tactical radios (and,
historically, a patent from Hedy Lamarr). It is a superb lesson in resilient communications: synchronisation, spread spectrum, and applied
cryptography, all on cheap radio modules.
WHAT THIS PROVES TO A RECRUITER
You understand frequency-hopping spread spectrum, transmitter and receiver hop synchronisation, why spreading resists jamming and
interception, and applying authenticated encryption (AES) to a real link. Resilient, secure communications is a core defense and aerospace EE
discipline.
→ the job this maps to: secure and resilient communications engineering — tactical-radio, aerospace-datalink, and
secure-IoT teams.
! SECURE YOUR OWN LINK, AND STAY LEGAL
Build this to protect communications you are allowed to operate, and stay within your local radio regulations — the legal band, power limits, and
any licensing. Resilient comms is about protecting your own link, not evading lawful authority. And never roll your own cryptography for anything
that matters; use a vetted AES implementation.

## how it works

▸
Spread spectrum, why: Concentrating a signal on one frequency makes it easy to jam and easy to intercept. Spreading it — hopping across many
channels — means a jammer must cover the whole band and an eavesdropper must know where to listen, dramatically improving resilience.

▸
Frequency hopping: Both ends step through a sequence of frequencies many times a second, following the same pseudo-random pattern seeded
by a shared secret. To anyone without the pattern, the signal appears as brief, scattered blips.

▸
Synchronisation is everything: The receiver must hop in lockstep with the transmitter. A shared clock or a sync handshake keeps them aligned;
lose sync and the link drops — which is why timing is the hardest part of the build.

▸
Encrypting the payload: Hopping hides where you transmit; encryption hides what you send. Wrapping each packet in authenticated AES means
even a receiver that follows the hops cannot read or forge the contents without the key.

▸
What the pros add: Real tactical radios add much faster hopping, wider bands, error correction, and rigorous key management. Your build captures
the core ideas honestly; the rest is scale and rigour.

## wiring at a glance (per node)
SIGNAL & POWER CONNECTIONS
→ ESP32 ↔ nRF24L01+ (PA/LNA) over SPI — SCK D18, MOSI D23, MISO D19, CSN D5, CE D4
→ 0.96" OLED on I²C — SDA D21, SCL D22

→ AES + hop schedule seeded by a shared key in firmware
## build steps

1
Build a plain link
Get two modules talking on a single fixed frequency first — send and receive packets reliably. Prove the basic radio before adding complexity.

2
Add channel hopping
Have both ends step through a list of channels on a shared schedule. Start slow, confirm they stay in sync, and watch packets get through as they
hop.

3
Synchronise robustly
Add a sync handshake so a receiver can find and lock onto the transmitter's hop sequence, and recover if it drifts. This is the make-or-break step.

4
Seed the pattern with a secret
Generate the hop sequence from a shared key so only the paired endpoints know the pattern. Confirm an unpaired receiver sees only scattered
blips.

5
Encrypt every packet
Wrap each payload in authenticated AES with the shared key. Verify the link still works end to end and that captured packets are unreadable without
the key.

Defense EE isn't about weapons
—
it's about who sees first.
A receiver pulling position from space, a needle pointing at a hidden transmitter, a dent in the magnetic field, footsteps through the ground, a drone's
own radio giving it away, a link that scatters and encrypts itself — six ways to detect, locate, navigate, and protect, without emitting harm. Every one
is receive-only, passive, or protective; the value is in the signal processing: the correlation, the phase, the anomaly detection, the synchronisation.
That is exactly what defense, aerospace, and spectrum teams hire for.
## the skill ladder
Build them in order and each one hands you the technique the next one needs:
SKILL LADDER
GNSS → direction finding → magnetic anomaly → seismic → passive RF detection → secure comms
! THE LINE THIS GUIDE STAYS ON
Everything here is receive-only, passive, or protective — built to detect, locate, navigate, and secure, never to jam, spoof, target, or harm. Jamming
or spoofing GNSS or drones is illegal and dangerous. Follow your local radio and privacy laws, keep the one transmitter here (the hopping link)
legal and within its band, and don't point these tools at people. Build to understand, and to protect.

Build even one. Capture it — a position track, a bearing swinging to a hidden transmitter, a magnetic anomaly map, a footstep trigger, a drone
flagged on a waterfall — and put the code on GitHub with your method, your results, and an honest note on scope and legal limits. One sensing
demo and one clean repo prove you can do defense-grade signal work.
